phase1.explanation:
You've technically met a few of these already, buried inside other lessons' broken code — this lesson just puts names to faces and lines them up together so you recognize them fast in the wild.

Most of what you'll hit day to day are unchecked, and they cluster around three themes. The first is [[key:missing or invalid data]]: [[term:NullPointerException]] happens the instant you call a method on a null reference — String str = null; str.length(); has nothing to call length() on. [[term:NumberFormatException]] is its cousin for parsing — Integer.parseInt("123abc") fails because that text simply isn't a valid number.

The second theme is [[key:going out of bounds]]: [[term:ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException]] for arrays, [[term:IndexOutOfBoundsException]] for Lists like ArrayList — both mean you asked for a position that doesn't actually exist in the collection, whether that's index 5 in a 3-element array or list.get(5) on a 3-element list.

The third is [[key:type and logic mistakes]]: [[term:ClassCastException]] fires when a downcast guesses wrong (we saw this back in Unit 2 with Animal/Dog/Cat), [[term:ArithmeticException]] covers math errors like dividing by zero, and [[term:IllegalArgumentException]] is the one YOU throw yourself, for a caller passing in a value your method simply can't work with — a negative age, for instance.

Then there's the checked side, which tends to show up specifically around I/O: [[term:IOException]] and its more specific subclass [[term:FileNotFoundException]] both cover things going wrong while reading or writing files — a missing file, a permission problem, a disk that's suddenly full. [[term:InterruptedException]] is checked too, and shows up when a thread gets interrupted while sleeping or waiting — we'll get there in a later unit.

[[warn:it's worth internalizing the pattern rather than memorizing this list]]: [[key:unchecked exceptions almost always mean a bug in your own code — fix the logic, don't just catch and ignore it]]. Checked exceptions usually mean something legitimately went wrong in the outside world, and THOSE are the ones genuinely worth a real try-catch with a meaningful recovery plan.
phase1.openingDialogue: Know your enemy — let's learn the most common exceptions~ 🐛

phase2.explanation:
No broken code this time — just two misconceptions worth correcting before they cause real confusion later.

First: [[warn:"NullPointerException means the variable is undefined" is wrong]]. The variable exists — it's just pointing at nothing. String str = null; is a completely valid, well-defined variable; it simply holds no object to call methods on, which is exactly why str.length() has nothing to work with.

Second: [[key:IOException isn't something to shrug off]]. Files go missing, disks fill up, permissions get denied — these happen constantly in real programs, far more often than most beginners expect, and every one of them deserves a genuine recovery plan (a retry, a fallback, a clear message to the user) rather than a catch block that just prints a stack trace and moves on.

phase3.openingDialogue: Quick quiz! Which exception is this? 🤔

mcq.question:
Which exception would be thrown by the following code?

String[] names = {"Alice", "Bob"};
System.out.println(names[2]);

A) NullPointerException
B) ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
C) NumberFormatException
D) ClassCastException
E) ArithmeticException

Select the correct exception.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: NullPointerException is so notoriously common that its inventor, Tony Hoare (who introduced the null reference concept back in 1965), has publicly called it his "billion-dollar mistake" — his own estimate of the cumulative cost of bugs it's caused across the software industry since.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
